items.title: Why a Tiny GPT Can Know Two Facts and Still Not Connect Them
items.summary: A "Two-Hop Curse" occurs when language models fail to connect two separate facts, even if they are present in the training data. This weakness is demonstrated by training a model on separate one-hop relationships, which causes it to fail when asked to compose the two facts. Introducing an "identity bridge"—an example mapping an entity to itself—helps the model learn to compose the facts. However, the benefit of this fix is temporary, as performance degrades over continued training. The experiment suggests that extended training allows the model to settle into separate representations for the facts, which is the mechanism behind the failure.

This method temporarily improved performance, but further training revealed that extended exposure allowed the model to develop separate representations for the facts, explaining the sustained difficulty in composition. This suggests that the mechanism behind the failure relates to the model's representation of individual facts rather than their relational connection. The findings indicate that architectural adjustments are necessary to improve factual synthesis in language models.

These changes led to significant time reductions in batch collection for specific tasks.
